content.text:
# Paint a picture

Paint a watercolor of the photograph in reference/.
The easel simulates watercolor on paper. The photograph is a Google Maps
screenshot, so leave out the map's panels, buttons, small inset map and logo
and paint what the photograph shows. Don't use image models.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/watercolor_easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift workable
  paint with a damp brush using `b:lift(path)`.
- You mix your own paint from the 36 library pigments with `b:load`, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(seconds)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/watercolor_easel_guide.md; notes/watercolor_techniques.md;
notes/research/watercolor_physics.md as needed.

## Working
Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.

After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Before adding repeated small details, improve a weakening relationship or deliberately accept it with your reason. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.

Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial, on the scratch sheet beside the painting (`scratch: true`) or on the painting, laid on the intended paper after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: paper and wetness, recipe ratios, water, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
  in your journal and finish.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

# Watercolor easel

The studio has five MCP tools: `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`.
`paint` runs a chunk of Lua. A chunk that succeeds keeps the paper, your
named brush loads and the material clock for the next chunk. A chunk that
fails leaves the committed painting as it was. Each chunk starts in a fresh
Lua VM: get your saved brushes back by name, and define your Lua variables
and functions again.
Lua's `io` library is unavailable; output uses `print`.

In the examples below, `<pigment>` stands for an id from `palette()`. Other
numbers in the examples show how a call is written; the values are yours to
choose.

## Paper and coordinates

```lua
paper{width=<cells>, height=<cells>, kind="<kind>", seed=<seed>}
```

- `width` and `height`: the sheet's size in simulation cells. Width accepts
  integers from 2 to 2,400 and height from 2 to 1,600.
- `kind`: `"cold-press"`, `"hot-press"` or `"rough"`.
- `seed`: an integer from 0 to 4,294,967,295.

The defaults are width 1,056, height 704, `"cold-press"` and seed 71, so
`paper{}` makes that sheet. The paper is created once; a continuation chunk
paints on the existing sheet. `paper{}` on a sheet that already has paper
stops the chunk with "paper already exists".

Coordinates and brush widths are in cells. The origin is the upper-left
corner; x increases to the right and y downward. Fractional coordinates are
allowed. The sheet's kind and seed set its tooth. The Watercolor Lab
simulation runs on a hardware GPU.

## Palette and brushes

`palette()` returns the ids of all 36 pigments in the library. Use those
exact strings in `b:load`. Each pigment carries its library values for
absorption, scattering, granulation, staining and density. A load mixes the
optical coefficients and material properties of its pigments in proportion
to the amounts still in the brush.

```lua
b = brush{name="<name>", width=<cells>}
```

This makes a named round brush. Width accepts 1 to 2,400 cells and defaults
to 24. Pressure changes the contact radius around that nominal width.
Calling `brush{name="<name>"}` again gets back its saved width and load; to
change the width, use a new name. A name has up to 80 letters, digits, `-`,
`_` and `.`. It can't start with `.`.

```lua
b:load{water=<microliters>, pigments={["<pigment>"]=<amount>}}
```

A load adds to what the brush already holds. Each call takes 0 to 100
microliters of water and 0 to 10 arbitrary mass units of each pigment, and
can load several pigments together. There is no cap on what a brush can
hold: five loads of 100 microliters leave it holding 500 microliters.
Strokes use the load up as they lay it, and the brush keeps what it hasn't
laid between strokes and chunks. `b:status()` reports its `width` and its
remaining `water` and `pigments`. A new name gives a clean, empty brush.
With a width-24 round at pressure 0.35 on cold-press paper, 40 µL water/1 French Ultramarine unit and 80 µL/2 units each carried a fading 936-cell stroke, leaving 3.30 and 9.01 µL.

## Marks and water

```lua
b:stroke({{x, y}, {x, y}, ...}, {pressure=<0..1>, duration=<seconds>})
```

A stroke takes a path of 1 to 2,000 points; a one-point path makes a round
contact. Pressure takes 0 to 1 and defaults to 0.35. A point can also be
`{x, y, pressure, time_seconds}`; point times start at zero and increase
along a moving path. Duration takes up to 600 seconds and must be positive
for a moving stroke. By default a stroke lasts its path length divided by
800 cells per second, with a minimum of 0.0625 seconds.

Water moves and dries during a stroke as its contacts are laid. `dry=true`
makes a dry contact and keeps the brush's water. A brush holding less than
0.001 microliters of water also makes a dry contact. `grade=<ratio>`, from
0 to 1, reduces the pigment from the top of a stroke to the bottom; 1 is an
even load.

`b:wash{x=, y=, width=, height=, grade=}` lays a rectangle as rows of brush
strokes. Its coordinates and dimensions are in cells. It takes the same
pressure, dry-contact, grade and duration options. Each row starts with the
brush's starting water and pigment load. That load is gradually replenished
along the row so a loaded brush can cover the rectangle. By default a row
lasts its length divided by 2,800 cells per second, with a minimum of
0.015625 seconds; `duration` sets the time of each row. A painting begun on
an earlier version of the easel keeps the wash timing it started with.

`drop{x=, y=, water=<microliters>, radius=<cells>}` adds clean water: 0 to
100 microliters. Radius accepts 1 to 1,200 cells, 12 by default. The water
lands as a soft patch that fades out 1.8 times the radius from the center.
Water can move workable paint and make a backrun. A drop lands at once and
takes no painter-clock time. A drop whose patch misses the sheet entirely
stops the chunk with "drop is outside paper". Stroke paths can run past the
edges. A painting begun on an earlier version of the easel keeps the drop
it started with, whose water stops at the radius.

`b:lift(path)` lays the round lift contact along a path of the same form.
It supplies water from the brush, loosens workable pigment on the sheet and
removes some suspended pigment from the sheet. Removed pigment is not added
to the brush's inventory. Cured paint has become part of the paper and
can't be lifted. `blot` and salt are unavailable here.

## Time and drying

`wait(seconds)` advances the material clock by 0 to 600 seconds a call and
returns the clock reading. `clock()` includes any fraction still waiting for
the next 0.0625-second tick. Each tick runs 11 or 12 Lab substeps, 180 per
painter-clock second on average. Looking and wall-clock time between calls
leave the material alone: the sheet stays as it was at the end of the last
call.

On the default paper, a test stroke on the Mac GPU became damp after about
1 second of further `wait` and dry after about 2.5 seconds, sampled every
0.25 seconds. It was a 150-cell stroke with a round brush of width 42 at
the default pressure 0.35, loaded with 10 microliters of water and 10 mass
units of French Ultramarine. The brush still held pigment when the stroke
ended. For a stroke like that, the wet-into-wet window is roughly the
first second of further painter-clock time. Earlier contacts in a stroke
have begun drying while the later ones are being laid.

Drying depends on the amount of water, the paper and the surrounding wet
area. A wetter area can stay workable longer.

`balance()` reports `dry`, `max_surface_water` and `max_wetness`, along with
diagnostics for the water and brush-release inventory. Standing surface
water at or below 0.002, with wetness remaining, counts as damp. `dry`
becomes true when wetness is below 0.02 everywhere and suspended pigment is at or
below 0.0001 per cell. The Lab reference uses half-float fields and
advection; `conserved` is false. The diagnostic totals don't promise
exact per-pigment conservation.

`glaze()` checks that the sheet is dry and refuses while it is wet. The
Lab engine already cures dry pigment into the paper's reflectance, so the
call adds no layer.

## Looking and the journal

The `look` tool returns a PNG of the paper as it is now. You see Color by
default. `mode: "gallery"` shows it in Gallery light (azimuth 115°,
elevation 55°, intensity 1) and `mode: "relief"` in raking light (135°,
25°, 1). A Color look also writes display-only Gallery and Relief
companions for the studio viewer, which shows Gallery light by default.
Looking changes neither the material nor the clock.

`size` sets the long side of a whole-sheet look, from 16 to 2,400 pixels.
Without it, the view has one pixel per cell. `crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1"` gives two
opposite corners in integer cells and returns that region at 1:1; `size`
has no effect on a crop. The `look` tool takes `mode`, `size`, `crop` and
`scratch`.

Within Lua, `look{path="<name>.png", mode="color", width=<pixels>}` writes a
PNG into the studio, from 1 to 2,400 pixels wide. A Lua crop is
`crop={x, y, width, height}` in output pixels. `save("<name>.json")`
captures the sheet, the clock and the brush loads under that name. Every
successful chunk also saves an automatic checkpoint, which the next chunk
loads. A chunk whose exact source has already run is refused, so each
continuation needs new code.

`note` appends an entry to `notes/journal.md`, stamped with the painting's
time. To revise an entry, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage
to change, which must appear there once, and `text`, what takes its
place. `status` reports the setup and the clock. `log` returns the
successful Lua chunks in order; they are also kept in
`paintings/lua/painting.lua`.

## The scratch paper

Beside the painting stands scratch paper for trying out a mix, a stroke,
a glaze or a drying time before it goes on the painting. `paint`, `look`,
`status` and `log` work on it with `scratch: true`; without it they work on
the painting.

- The first use sets it up as the painting's paper was set up: the same
  size, kind and seed. The painting needs its own `paper{}` first. Each
  scratch sheet, the first and every fresh one, comes with its paper, so
  scratch chunks start without `paper{}`.
- It is a separate sheet with its own brushes, loads, clock and log,
  `paintings/lua/scratch.lua`. Load a brush again here. Nothing done on
  it reaches the painting.
- It keeps its own clock. Time spent or waited there doesn't pass for
  the painting, and the painting's time doesn't pass for it.
- To use what worked, paint it on the painting with the same handling.
- `new_scratch: true`, with `scratch: true`, puts the current sheet aside
  and starts a fresh one before the chunk runs. The old log stays as
  `paintings/lua/scratch-1.lua`, then `scratch-2.lua` and so on. Each has
  its final checkpoint beside it as `scratch-1.json`, `scratch-2.json` and
  so on, so an operator can render that sheet later.
- A trial judges a passage only as far as it repeats that passage's
  conditions: lay the underlayer you mean to work over, and let it dry
  as long as it has on the painting.

## Lua

Lua has the math, table, string and utf8 libraries, a 128 MB memory limit
and a budget of about two million instructions per chunk. Native painting
and waiting run outside that instruction budget. Keep the same runner build
when continuing a painting.

A `paint` call has 12 minutes of wall time, on either sheet. A chunk still
running at 12 minutes is stopped, and the call replies "the easel didn't
answer; `log` shows whether the chunk ran". Wall time grows with the number
of stroke calls more than with their length. In the first watercolor sitting,
on the Mac GPU at 1,056 × 704 cells, stroke calls took about 0.3 seconds
each: chunks of 1,100 to 1,300 strokes took 5 to 8 minutes, and a chunk of
about 3,900 strokes was stopped. The sheet stays as it was between chunks,
so a long pass can continue in the next chunk while its paint is still wet.

# Watercolor techniques at this easel

How the watercolor painter's techniques are done with this easel's tools, and
where the engine differs from real paper. `notes/watercolor_easel_guide.md`
says what each call does; `notes/research/watercolor_physics.md` says how real
watercolor behaves. What you paint is yours to choose. In the examples,
`<pigment>` stands for any id that `palette()` returns.

## Plan before you paint

- **Try it on the scratch paper** (`scratch: true`): a load, a stroke, a wash
  into wet paper, a lift. The scratch sheet has the painting's size, kind and
  seed, and its own brushes and clock. Lay the underlayer the trial will go
  over and give it the same waiting time as on the painting, then compare
  the two in a 1:1 crop. Paint what worked on the painting with the same
  load, path, pressure and timing.
- **Start a clean sheet** with `new_scratch: true` when the scratch paper is
  full or when a trial needs dry, untouched paper.
- **Look at 1:1.** `look` with `crop="x0,y0,x1,y1"` returns cells at 1:1,
  which shows edges, granulation and dry-brush breaks. `mode="relief"` rakes
  light across the tooth. Looking does not advance the clock.

## Paper

- `paper{kind="hot-press"}`, `"cold-press"` (the default) or `"rough"` is
  chosen once, before the first mark. In this engine the kind sets the
  height of the tooth (relative amplitude 0.3 hot-press, 0.72 cold-press,
  1.0 rough) and its fiber texture. Absorption, evaporation and capillary
  spread use the same settings on all three kinds; there is no sizing
  setting.
- `seed=` changes the pattern of the tooth. The scratch paper copies it.

## Time and the stages of wetness

- **The clock is fast.** Real paper takes minutes to pass from shiny to dry
  (the physics note's table). Here a measured stroke went from wet to damp in
  about **1 second** of painter-clock `wait` and to dry in about **2.5
  seconds**, sampled every 0.25 seconds. That stroke was a 150-cell round
  stroke on the default paper, width 42, pressure 0.35, loaded with
  10 microliters of water and 10 mass units of `french-ultramarine`. A wetter or
  larger area stays workable longer.
- **The stroke dries as it is laid.** Point times and `duration` are painter
  clock too. In a slow stroke the first contacts have begun drying before
  the last ones land. Give a stroke that should stay wet along its length a
  short duration.
- **Broad areas.** In the first watercolor sitting, rows of short
  topped-up strokes on dry paper (6 µL per top-up, width 80) lost their
  standing water within about 2 seconds of the last stroke and were dry
  within about 4. A pre-wet grid of `drop{}` (radius 80, about
  118 × 95 cells apart) kept the area wet for 2 to 4 seconds after the last
  stroke at 5 to 8 µL a drop. A 22 µL grid (radius 85, about 118 × 100
  cells apart) kept it wet for about 12 seconds. Those drops were laid on
  an earlier version of the easel, where a drop's water stopped at its
  radius. Nine
  rows across the whole 1,056-cell width of the sheet, laid in 25-cell
  segments at 3,500 cells a second, took 2.8 seconds of painter clock.
  Rows that took 4 seconds to lay over a 4 µL pre-wet showed bands where
  they landed late; rows laid in 2.8 seconds over a 5 µL pre-wet blended.
- **Reading the stage.** `balance()` returns `max_surface_water`,
  `max_wetness` and `dry`. Standing water above 0.002 means some of the
  sheet is still wet; 0.002 or less with wetness left is damp; `dry` is true when wetness
  is below 0.02 everywhere and suspended pigment is at or below 0.0001 per
  cell everywhere. These are maxima over the whole sheet, so any
  wet passage elsewhere sets them. To time one passage, lay it alone on the
  scratch paper and step the clock. What a chunk prints comes back in the
  `paint` reply:

  ```lua
  for i = 1, 16 do
    local t = wait(0.25)
    local s = balance()
    print(t, s.max_surface_water, s.max_wetness, s.dry)
  end
  ```

- Wall-clock time between calls and looking leave the sheet as it was.

## Loading and laying paint

- `b = brush{name="<name>", width=<cells>}` makes a round brush; the same name
  later returns it with its remaining load. A new name is a clean brush.
- `b:load{water=<µL>, pigments={["<pigment>"]=<mass>}}` adds to the load.
  The brush releases water and pigment from what it holds, and `b:status()`
  shows what is left. A standalone stroke can run dry before its path ends.
- `b:stroke(path, {pressure=..., duration=...})`. Each point can carry its own
  pressure and time, `{x, y, pressure, t}`. Pressure widens or narrows the
  contact around the nominal width.
- `b:wash{x=, y=, width=, height=}` lays a rectangle as rows of strokes and
  replenishes the brush's starting load along each row. By default a row
  lasts its length divided by 2,800 cells per second, with a minimum of
  0.015625 seconds; `duration=` sets the time of each row. A painting begun
  on an earlier version of the easel keeps the wash timing it started with.
  `grade=` thins the pigment from top to bottom (`1` is even).

## Broad areas

What the first watercolor sitting found when it covered large areas with
rows of strokes:

- **A fresh load lands heaviest at the start of the next stroke.** With
  width-60 brushes, 20 µL per 120-cell segment left a bloom at every
  segment start, and 8 µL per 60 cells was nearly even. Topping the brush
  up to a fixed load of 2 to 6 µL every 10 to 30 cells laid an even band.
  To top up, load the difference between the target and what `b:status()`
  reports.
- **Every segment is a stroke call**, and stroke calls set a chunk's wall
  time (see the easel guide's Lua section).
- **Row edges show.** Neighboring rows of one mix laid in quick succession
  on dry paper merged. Where a row ended it left a hard, slightly ragged
  edge, and rows laid after their neighbors had dried showed as stripes.
  Short stacked rows read as flat bars with rounded ends.
- **A light pre-wet joins the rows.** A grid of 5 µL drops (radius 80,
  about 118 × 95 cells apart) laid just before the rows let neighboring
  rows blend while the colors stayed roughly in place. At 22 µL a drop the
  pigment traveled across the wet area and piled up at its boundary. These
  drops were laid on an earlier version of the easel, where a drop's water
  stopped at its radius.

## Wet-in-wet

- **Wet the area first.** Make a fresh named brush and load it with water
  only (`w = brush{name="<new name>"}; w:load{water=<µL>}`); a used brush
  keeps the pigment it still holds. Lay a wash or stroke with it, or put down clean water with
  `drop{x=, y=, water=<µL>, radius=<cells>}`. Then lay the pigment while the
  area is still wet: for a stroke-sized area that is within about a second
  of painter clock, longer for a flooded one.
- **Charge a wet stroke.** A second loaded brush laid into a stroke that is
  still wet joins its water, and the two loads flow together where they
  meet.
- **Mixtures.** A brush carrying several pigments lays one blended color with
  the averaged granulation, staining and density of its load. Where two
  colors meet wet, each cell carries one blended set as well. Pigments in a
  mixture do not separate by density here.

## Edges and backruns

- **Hard edges.** Water evaporates faster at the boundary of a wet area, and
  pigment there settles out as it dries, so a stroke laid on dry paper dries
  with a darker rim.
- **Soft edges.** Lay the stroke into wet paper, or into the still-wet edge of
  the passage beside it, before either reaches damp.
- **Backruns (blooms).** Clean water or a wetter load added to paint that has
  lost its standing water but is still damp spreads into it and pushes
  pigment to a darker, lobed rim. `drop{}` is the direct way. The wetness of
  damp paper fades over time, so the window for a backrun is short at this
  clock. Find it on the scratch paper with the same load and wait.
- Water dropped on dry paint finds nothing to move (see Glazing).

## Granulation

- Granulating pigments settle into the valleys of the tooth, most in slow,
  shallow water. The texture is fixed into the paper when the cell dries and
  stays visible under later glazes. A taller tooth (rough) gives stronger
  settling. The engine has no separate flocculation; clumping shows only as
  this settling.
- The engine's library values, with its own thresholds for these words:

| Property | Pigment ids |
|---|---|
| Granulating (0.5 or more) | `yellow-ochre`, `cobalt-violet`, `ultramarine-violet`, `french-ultramarine`, `cobalt-blue`, `cerulean-blue`, `viridian`, `terre-verte`, `raw-sienna`, `burnt-sienna`, `raw-umber`, `burnt-umber`, `indian-red`, `buff-titanium` |
| Staining (0.65 or more) | `indian-yellow`, `pyrrol-scarlet`, `quinacridone-rose`, `alizarin-crimson`, `quinacridone-burnt-orange`, `dioxazine-violet`, `phthalo-blue`, `prussian-blue`, `indanthrone-blue`, `phthalo-green` |
| Opaque (scattering 1.2 or more): can cover the color beneath and lighten darker passages, depending on the load | `cadmium-yellow`, `naples-yellow`, `cadmium-orange`, `cadmium-red`, `cerulean-blue`, `indian-red`, `buff-titanium` |
| Light (density 0.3 or less): stays in the water and travels far in blooms | `hansa-yellow`, `indian-yellow`, `green-gold`, `pyrrol-scarlet`, `quinacridone-rose`, `alizarin-crimson`, `quinacridone-burnt-orange`, `dioxazine-violet`, `phthalo-blue`, `prussian-blue`, `indanthrone-blue`, `phthalo-green`, `sap-green`, `hookers-green`, `neutral-tint` |

## Lifting

- `b:lift(path)` lays water from the brush along the path and loosens
  pigment that has settled but not dried. The lift loosens pigment only
  where there is water on the paper, so load the brush with water and it
  brings its own. Its scrub effect fades within a fraction of a second of
  painter clock.
- Staining pigment resists the lift and gives up only part of its deposit;
  non-staining pigment lifts nearly clean.
- **Lifting loosens workable pigment and removes some suspension from the
  sheet.** Removed pigment is not added to the brush's inventory. Loosened
  pigment that stays moves with the water and settles again. There is no
  blotting (`blot` is unavailable).
- **Dry paint cannot be lifted.** Once a cell is dry its paint is part of the
  paper. Lift before the area dries.

## Glazing

- Wait until `balance().dry` is true (or `glaze()` succeeds; it refuses while
  the sheet is wet). A stroke over dry paint then lays a new
  layer whose color combines with what is under it.
- Dried paint here does not redissolve: water and new paint over it leave it
  as it is, so a glaze never stirs the layer beneath. Real paint can
  redissolve and tint the new layer (the physics note's staining section).
- Opaque pigments can cover the color beneath and lighten darker passages;
  how much depends on the load. Transparent ones let what is under them show
  through. Try a glaze over the same
  underlayer on the scratch paper first.
- **Weak mixes vanish over dark or strong passages.** In the first watercolor
  sitting, over a dried `burnt-umber` and `french-ultramarine` passage,
  `buff-titanium` and `naples-yellow` at 0.1 to 0.15 units per 2.5 to
  3 µL disappeared, and 0.6 to 0.8 units per 1.5 µL showed as light marks.
  Over the same passage, dark lines from brushes 2 to 9 cells wide needed
  about 0.25 to 0.35 `sepia` with 0.2 to 0.25 `french-ultramarine` per
  0.4 to 1 µL; 0.15 `sepia` with 0.1 `french-ultramarine` hardly showed at
  width 2. A glaze
  of 0.03 `quinacridone-rose` with 0.012 `french-ultramarine` per 2.2 µL
  barely changed a dried `cobalt-blue` and `buff-titanium` passage.

## Dry brush

- `b:stroke(path, {dry=true})`, or a brush with almost no water left, makes
  dry contact: pigment lands on the high points of the tooth and skips the
  valleys. The brush keeps its water. The paper's kind and seed decide
  where the stroke breaks.
- Pressure changes the contact width. Check the mark in a 1:1 crop and in
  `relief`, on the scratch paper first.

## Limits of this engine

- **One dried layer.** Every dried pass folds into a single paper
  reflectance. The engine keeps no separate glaze layers and no record of
  which pigment lies where once it has dried.
- **No blotting** and no salt. Neither call is available.
- **Pigment is not conserved while it flows.** The amount of pigment can
  drift as paint moves with the water; `balance()` reports
  `conserved=false`.
- **No sizing or tilt.** Paper kinds differ in tooth and fiber texture, and
  no call tilts the sheet or changes its sizing.
- **Fast clock.** Stages that take minutes on real paper pass in seconds
  here, so time wet work by `balance()` and scratch trials.

## Finishing

- Let the sheet dry (`balance().dry`) before the final looks; a last
  `paint` chunk can `wait` and print `balance().dry`.
- The brief's final look in normal color is a whole-sheet `look` and
  detail crops, all without `mode`, taken after the last `paint` call on the
  painting. A `paint` call on the painting after them, even one that only
  waits or prints, means taking them again. `paint` calls on the scratch
  sheet leave them standing.
- Gallery and Relief looks are extra views. The studio viewer shows the
  painting in Gallery light by default; `look` with `mode="gallery"` shows
  the same.

# Physics of transparent watercolor on paper

**Tags.** **[V]**: the statement or number is in the source text. **[S]**: it is from a summary of the source, or it is a practitioner's observation reported by the source. **[E]**: an estimate or inference, with its assumptions stated.

Watercolor paint is pigment dispersed in a water-soluble binder, usually gum arabic[V]; vegetable gums, dextrin and tragacanth also occur[V]. The paper and the water on it decide most of what the paint does.

---

## 1. Paper: sizing and surface

**Sizing.** Internal sizing is added to the pulp, mainly to make the sheet less wettable. Surface sizing is a film applied after the sheet is formed. A heavily sized sheet is called hard-sized and a lightly sized one soft- or slack-sized. A sheet made with no size (waterleaf) is very absorbent[V]. Watercolor papers usually carry a surface coat of gelatin or starch, and rarely the synthetic size Aquapel, thin to moderately heavy[V]. One paper maker describes internal sizing as limiting how far pigment is absorbed and keeping colors transparent[V].

- On a dry sheet the paint bonds mostly to the sizing layer on the surface, and on gelatin-sized paper a mistake can be scraped or dissolved away with the size[V].
- Light wetting loosens the surface size and raises the fibers slightly[S]. Soaking can soften or remove water-soluble sizing; the effect depends on the sizing material[S].
- A painter's account: heavily sized paper gives brighter color, sharper edges, stronger granulation, easier blooms and easier lifting; lightly sized paper absorbs paint quickly, gives softer edges and paler color, dries faster and takes layers more easily[S].

**Surface.** Papers come in three finishes: rough, cold-pressed and hot-pressed[V]. Hot-pressed paper is pressed between iron rollers, which closes the spaces between fibers and makes it less absorbent. It often gets a lighter surface size, so staining paints can stain it aggressively and scraping shows more[V]. Cold-pressed paper has a light texture and is the most common finish[V]. Heavier sheets of the same nominal finish usually have a coarser texture[V]. A paper maker's dry-brush test: on a smooth sheet the touch of color is uniform; on a fine-grain (cold-pressed) sheet it breaks slightly with irregular edges; on rough paper it misses the dips[V].

**Weight.** Watercolor papers run from about **190 to 800 g/m²**. Heavier paper holds moisture longer, so paint on it dries more slowly; sheets under 300 g/m² buckle sooner[V].

## 2. Water on the sheet: stages and timing

Handprint describes six stages of paper wetness from its author's own observation, timed from a generous wash of water on level dry paper under ordinary studio heat and humidity[S]:

| Stage | First appears | What the paper does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Soaked | 0 min | Covered by about 1.5–3 mm of water; it flows to the low edge at the slightest tilt. Diluted paint spreads to about twice the brushed area |
| Shiny | +2 min | Shiny, with the texture visible. Diluted paint spreads to about 1.5 times the brushed area; clean water dropped into a wash leaves a large backrun |
| Satin | +4 min | A dull satin luster hides the texture; little flow when tilted. Diluted paint gives soft backruns; clean water dropped into a wash lifts a light spot |
| Moist | +7 min | Looks just dried but feels cool. Diluted paint gives crisp backruns; paint has begun to dry lighter and duller |

| Damp | +10 min | Looks and feels dry; water is still deep in the sheet. Effects are slight and unpredictable, and watery paint can still bloom |
| Dry | +20 min | New paint flows and dries normally; the underlying wash produces no wet-in-wet backrun. The shift to the dry color is complete |

Actual drying speed depends on the amount of water, the absorbency of the paper, the temperature and the relative humidity[S]. Other teachers count different stages; Zbukvic names four: wet, moist, damp and dry[S].

**Damp paper.** Water added to a damp sheet sinks into its wet core and comes back up through the fibers, so blotches and wrinkled backruns appear inside and along the painted area. These come from inside the paper, so lifting the surface paint does not remove them[S].

**Dry shift.** Wet paint looks dark and intense, and it dulls and lightens as it dries. The shift starts around the moist stage and is complete when the sheet is dry[S].

## 3. Wet-in-wet spread

Paint laid on a sheet already wet with water spreads freely into soft, feathery shapes, with fine striations that follow the flow of the water[V]. How far it spreads depends on the paper's wetness and on the dilution of the paint (the table above). Thick paint on shiny paper gives a crinkled edge with a large fringe and dries slowly[S].

## 4. Edges and backruns

**Edge darkening.** A stroke laid on dry paper does not spread, because the sizing and the surface tension of the water hold its edge in place. As it dries, pigment moves from the interior toward that edge and leaves a darker line there[V]. The edge stays pinned, so water evaporating near it is replaced by water flowing outward from the interior, and that flow carries pigment along[V]. The same capillary flow leaves the ring of a dried coffee drop, where evaporation is fastest at the pinned edge[S]. Paint makers formulate watercolors so that this edge forms[V].

**Backruns (blooms).** When water spreads back into a damp area of paint, as when a wash dries unevenly, it pushes pigment ahead of it and leaves branching shapes with strongly darkened edges[V]. Handprint's account of how to get more or fewer of them[V]:

- More: satin or moist paper, a level sheet, more water from a large full brush and more diluted paint.
- Fewer: paper that is fully dry or fully wet, a slight tilt, excess water wicked from the bottom of a fresh area, a smaller or drier brush and thicker paint.

Low-absorbency sheets, including many hot-pressed papers, produce backruns more readily[V]. Handprint's blossoming test rewets a moderately diluted layer, allowed to dry until nonreflective, with clear water; paints differ in how far they redissolve and move[V].

## 5. Granulation, flocculation and separation

- **Granulation** is a grainy texture that follows the peaks and valleys of the paper. It varies by pigment and is strongest when the paper is very wet[V]. It is tied to the pigment's specific gravity, through sedimentation[V]. Rough paper strengthens it because pigment settles into the crevices[V]; a cratered rough finish pooled granular pigments (cobalts, ultramarine, cadmiums) more than any other moderately priced paper tested[V].
- **Flocculation** is a clumping of pigment into tiny flakes or spots, as in ultramarine blue. Handprint rates it together with granulation on a 0–4 scale[V]. Granulation medium produces a flocculated texture even in paints that wash smooth[V].
- **Separation**: in a mixture, the denser pigment settles first and the colors split[V].

Manufacturer ratings for some common pigments[V]:

| Pigment (Colour Index) | Granulation | Staining | Transparency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ultramarine blue (PB29) | Granulating | Medium | Transparent |
| Cobalt blue (PB28) | Granulating | Low | Semi-transparent |
| Cerulean blue (PB35) | Granulating | Non-staining | Semi-transparent |
| Burnt sienna (PBr7) | Granulating | Non-staining | Semi-transparent |
| Transparent red oxide (PR101) | Granulating | Non-staining | Transparent |
| Phthalo blue (PB15:3) | Non-granulating | High | Transparent |
| Phthalo green (PG7) | Non-granulating | High | Transparent |

## 6. Staining and lifting

Handprint measures staining by drying a stroke of paint diluted about 1:3, wiping it five times with a wet swab and rating what remains, from 0 (lifts completely) to 4 (heavy, indelible stain)[V]. Staining comes from the pigment, the paint and the paper together[V]:

- Very small particles lodge between paper fibers too deep to wipe out, and some cling electrostatically[V].
- Dispersants such as ox gall and humectants carry pigment deeper into the fibers[V].
- Paint rich in gum arabic holds the pigment on the surface in a coating that redissolves, so it lifts more easily[V].
- Heavier sizing keeps pigment on the surface; lightly sized, rough and loosely beaten papers stain more[V].

Any staining paint can redissolve when wetted again and tint the next layer[V].

## 7. Transparency and glazing

**Transparency.** In watercolor, light passes mostly between pigment particles: a sparse layer of small particles covers less of the paper. Very little light passes through the particles themselves[V]. How much light a pigment scatters depends on the ratio between its refractive index and that of the medium around it. Gum arabic (about **1.47**) is close to some pigments and to the clear substrates that many organic pigments are bound to, which cuts the white scatter at their surfaces. A refractive index above about 1.5 counts as relatively hiding[V]:

| Pigment | Refractive index |
| --- | --- |
| Phthalocyanines | 1.4 |
| Ultramarine blue | 1.6 |
| Cobalt blue | 1.7 |
| Cerulean blue | 1.8 |
| Cadmium yellow | 2.4 |

What watercolor painters call transparency the paint industry calls low hiding power. Handprint tests it by painting over black lines and comparing them with a line drawn across the dried swatch[V].

**Glazing.** A glaze is a thin layer laid after the layer beneath has dried. The colors mix optically, through their superposition on the paper, and paints with low resolubility let a dried wash take a new layer without lifting[V]. Curtis and colleagues composite such layers with the Kubelka–Munk model[V]. In Handprint's own test, the same total amount of pigment laid in one, two or four layers gave swatches that looked no darker or richer for the extra layers[S].

## 8. Dry brush

A nearly dry brush, drawn at a low angle, leaves paint only on the raised parts of rough paper, with irregular gaps and ragged edges[V]. The coarser the surface, the more the stroke breaks (section 1)[V].

## 9. Salt

Salt sprinkled into a wet wash absorbs water and leaves the pigment to settle into the paper. Fine table salt gives small speckles; larger rock salt pulls in more paint and gives bigger star-shaped marks. The salt is brushed off once the paint is dry[V].

local function interp(P, x)
  if x <= P[1][1] then return P[1][2] end
  for i=1,#P-1 do local a,b=P[i],P[i+1]
    if x>=a[1] and x<=b[1] then return a[2]+(b[2]-a[2])*(x-a[1])/(b[1]-a[1]) end end
  return P[#P][2]
end
local topP = {{0,226},{90,250},{177,278},{250,305},{319,332},{360,360},{400,382},{450,404},{500,420},{540,438},{584,448},{650,452},{714,456}}
local function trailR(y) return 714 + math.max(0,(y-456))*1.18 end
local function litf(x,y)
  local ax, ay = 300, 240
  local L = math.sqrt(ax*ax+ay*ay)
  local u = ((x-640)*ax + (y-470)*ay)/L/L
  local v = ((x-640)*(-ay) + (y-470)*ax)/L/ 150
  local w = 1 - math.abs(v)
  if u < -0.15 then w = w - (-0.15-u)*3 end
  return math.max(0, math.min(1, w*1.5))
end
local am = {["burnt-umber"]=0.02, ["sepia"]=0.006, ["french-ultramarine"]=0.006}

-- Campaign 39: valley patchwork - light fields and dark hedgerows, scaled with distance
local function trailR(y) return 714 + math.max(0,(y-456))*1.18 end
local function top(b, mx, target, f)
  local need = target - b:status().water
  if need > 0 then local p={} for k,v in pairs(mx) do p[k]=v*need*(f or 1) end; b:load{water=need, pigments=p} end
end
local seed = 4040
local function rnd() seed = (seed*1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648; return seed/2147483648 end
local F = brush{name="fields_light", width=14}
local fm = {["buff-titanium"]=0.06, ["green-gold"]=0.03, ["sap-green"]=0.02, ["yellow-ochre"]=0.01}
local H = brush{name="hedges", width=6}
local hm = {["hookers-green"]=0.08, ["paynes-gray"]=0.04, ["terre-verte"]=0.03}
for k=1,60 do
  local y = 400 + (rnd()^1.3)*300
  local d = (y - 390)/310        -- 0 far, 1 near
  local x = trailR(y) + 30 + rnd()*(1180 - trailR(y))
  if x < 1175 then
    local len = 20 + 70*d*(0.5+rnd())
    local th = 2 + 6*d
    if rnd() < 0.5 then
      top(F, fm, 0.4 + 0.8*d, 0.5 + 0.5*d)
      F:stroke({{x,y,0.25+0.2*d},{x+len, y+(rnd()-0.5)*th, 0.25+0.2*d}}, {duration=0.04})
    else
      top(H, hm, 0.3 + 0.4*d, 0.4 + 0.7*d)
      H:stroke({{x,y,0.3+0.2*d},{x+len*0.5, y+(rnd()-0.5)*2, 0.3},{x+len, y+(rnd()-0.5)*3, 0.25}}, {duration=0.04})
    end
  end
end

content.text:
**Red Path above the Plain**

This is a watercolor of the Google Maps view, painted from a spot on the mountain trail. A dark red volcanic slope fills the lower left. A paler gravel path runs from a small pile of dark lava rocks on the rim down toward the viewer. Above it, a bank of green trees and a grey boulder climb into a stormy blue sky. To the right, the land drops away to hazy blue ridges and a wide green plain, broken by faint field and hedge strokes. I left out the map panels, buttons, inset map and logo.

**Unresolved passages:**
- The slope and trail still read as overlapping oval dabs, like scales, rather than gravel.
- A rectangular haze block is still visible at the horizon, around x 500–830, y 330–390.
- The dark clumps in the trees look like blobs.
- The rocks on the rim look like a pile of cookies.
- A few white specks in the sky near the trees (around x 280–330, y 120) were never covered.
- The upper sky is heavier and darker than the photograph's.

**What worked, and the conditions:**
- **Flat, even areas (sky, valley, haze):** a grid of 4 µL water drops (radius 70–78, about 100 × 85 cells apart). Then a width 40–50 brush, topped up to 2.5–3 µL every 28–30 cells, laying 32–34-cell segments at 0.03 s each. This only held up when the whole area went down in about 3 seconds.
- **Breaking up row stripes:** short strokes laid at random angles worked better than glazing in rows. The trial used a width-34 brush, 2 µL per load, and 0.015 indian red plus 0.02 burnt umber per µL.
- **Soft cloud streaks:** lift strokes with pressure rising and falling along the path (1.2–2.5 µL water, width 24–30, 0.25 s), laid right after the sky wash.

**What failed, and my best explanation:**
- Row glazes laid in wetted bands over large soil areas left hard stripes at the joins. My hypothesis is that each band dried before the next one arrived. Don't retry them over big areas.
- Dabbing paint into a sky wash that was already drying left round bloom marks.
- A clean-water stroke laid under a still-wet ridge stroke lifted the paint instead of softening the edge.
- Opaque buff-titanium covers hid the dark soil but left visible dabs. A semi-opaque warm glaze afterwards only partly merged them, so the scale problem above is still open.
- Practical: a paint chunk with roughly 1,000 or more stroke calls ran past the 12-minute limit and was stopped. Keep each chunk under about 900 strokes.

All of this is recorded in the journal.
